title: Scalar and binary quantization
summary: int8 costs 0.6 points of recall for 4x compression with no training, which makes it close to free. Binary at the same byte budget as PQ loses on raw recall but needs 12 instructions per comparison instead of 96, and once a rescoring stage runs the accuracy difference between all three largely disappears.
html:
Product quantization needed codebooks, k-means, a rotation and a lookup table. Today has two methods with no training at all, and one of them is close to free money.

Scalar quantization: just use fewer bits

Find each dimension's range across the corpus, divide it into 256 buckets, store a byte:

lo, hi = X.min(axis=0), X.max(axis=0)
scale  = (hi - lo) / 255

code   = round((x - lo) / scale)        # uint8
approx = code * scale + lo

Four times smaller, no training, about six lines. Measured on the usual 6,200 embeddings:

float32 exact              1536 B    1x    recall@10  1.000
int8 scalar quantization    384 B    4x    recall@10  0.994   (0.999 with rescoring)

Six tenths of one percent of recall, for a quarter of the memory. There is no tuning, nothing to get wrong, and the error is bounded per dimension rather than depending on how well a codebook happened to fit.

If you take one practical thing from this phase, make it this: int8 is close to free and most systems should have it on by default. It is the cheapest row in the whole table.

Binary: one bit per dimension

Push it to the limit and keep only the sign:

code = (x > 0)            # 384 dims -> 384 bits -> 48 bytes, 32x smaller

Comparing two codes is a Hamming distance, which on a 64 bit machine is 6 XORs and 6 POPCNT instructions for 384 dimensions. That is about as cheap as a comparison gets.

It also loses a lot:

binary, Hamming (both sides 1-bit)    48 B   32x   recall@10  0.595

Which brings back Day 22's lesson. You quantized the query, and you did not have to. Keep the query in float and score it against the sign codes instead:

binary, float query (asymmetric)      48 B   32x   recall@10  0.707

Eleven points, for keeping information you already had. The same mistake and the same fix as symmetric versus asymmetric distance in PQ. If you implement binary quantization and skip this, you are leaving a sixth of your recall on the floor.

Why throwing away the magnitudes hurts less than it should

Pause on how violent binary quantization is. A 384 dimension vector of carefully fitted floats becomes 384 yes-or-no answers. Every magnitude is gone. The model spent a hundred million parameters deciding that dimension 97 should be 0.0031 rather than 0.0029, and you have replaced that with "positive".

That it retains any useful signal at all comes from dimensionality. Two random unit vectors in 384 dimensions agree on roughly half their signs, and the fraction of signs two vectors share is a decent estimate of the angle between them. You are not measuring each dimension well, you are measuring 384 of them badly and averaging, and the averaging does most of the work.

Which also tells you when binary stops working: low dimensions. At 64 dimensions there are not enough sign bits to average over and the estimate gets noisy. The method gets better as vectors get wider, which is the opposite of most compression intuitions and worth remembering when you meet a 3072 dimension model.

The head to head nobody runs

Binary at 1 bit per dimension and PQ at m=48 both land on exactly 48 bytes for a 384 dimension vector, so they can be compared directly:

method                            bytes   raw recall   with rescore-100
binary, Hamming                      48        0.595              0.967
binary, float query                  48        0.707              0.997
PQ m=48                              48        0.769              0.999

PQ wins on raw recall, which makes sense: it spends its 48 bytes on learned centroids rather than on throwing away every magnitude in the vector.

Now look at the right hand column. Once a rescoring stage re-ranks a hundred candidates with full vectors, the three methods land at 0.967, 0.997 and 0.999. Two of them are indistinguishable and the third is close.

So in the architecture you would actually build, the accuracy argument between these largely evaporates, and the decision moves somewhere else.

Where the decision actually lives

Cost per candidate, which Day 15 taught you to count in bytes rather than operations:

                   bytes/vector   ops per comparison    GB touched (200k vectors)
float32                    1536   384 multiply-adds                        0.307
int8                        384   384 cheap ops                            0.077
PQ ADC m=48                  48   48 lookups + 48 adds                     0.010
binary Hamming               48   6 XOR + 6 POPCNT                         0.010

Binary and PQ touch the same memory, because they store the same number of bytes. The difference is entirely in the arithmetic: 12 instructions against 96, and the twelve are the cheapest instructions on the chip with no table to keep in cache.

That is binary's whole case. Not smaller, not more accurate, just brutally fast per comparison, which matters when you are filtering an enormous candidate set before anything smarter runs.

I did measure wall clock and the numbers were useless: float32 came out fastest because numpy hands it to BLAS while my Hamming path is a numpy lookup table rather than a real POPCNT. Same artefact as Days 16 and 22. The bytes and instruction counts are the part that transfers.

What to actually use

  • int8, always. 4x for half a percent. There is no argument against it and no tuning to get wrong.
  • Binary as a first filter at very large scale, where you can afford to pull a deep candidate list and rescore it. Its recall alone is poor and that does not matter if it is stage one of three.
  • PQ when you need a specific byte budget. It is the only one of the three where you choose the compression ratio. Binary is fixed at d/8 bytes and int8 at d bytes, take it or leave it.

The combination you will see in real systems is binary or PQ for the first pass, int8 for the rescoring vectors, and full precision only if something downstream genuinely needs it. Three tiers, each an order of magnitude bigger and slower than the last, which is the same shape as every cache hierarchy you have ever worked with.

Everything in Phase 2 so far shrinks a vector by throwing information away after the model has produced it. Tomorrow is a different idea: train the model so that the first half of the vector is already a usable vector. Matryoshka embeddings.
exercise:
1. Implement int8 and confirm it is free. Six lines: per-dimension min and max, scale to 0-255, round, then reconstruct. Measure recall@10 against your float32 baseline. If you lose more than about one point, check you are scaling per dimension rather than globally, because a single global range is much worse and it is the usual mistake.

2. Prove the asymmetric gap for yourself. Build sign-bit codes for your corpus. Score queries two ways, once as Hamming distance against binarised queries and once as a float dot product against the sign codes. The gap was 11 points for me and it costs nothing to collect.

3. Price your three tiers. For your corpus size, compute total bytes at binary, PQ with your chosen m, int8, and float32. Decide which tiers live in RAM and which on disk, using Day 25's accounting. That four row table is the memory architecture of your retrieval system, and it fits on a napkin.
